zones.name: Borgo Panigale-Reno
zones.text: Bologna's western edge, residential and industrial, well away from anything a visitor comes for — the Ducati works and the airport approach are here. Local reporting on the quartiere identifies Barca and Casteldebole, the parts with the weakest socio-economic profile, as more exposed to drug dealing; the rest is unremarkable suburb. Few travellers stay here and there is little reason to walk it at night.

zones.name: Navile
zones.text: Bolognina and the northern side of the station — where a lot of Bologna's cheaper hotels are — and the single most heavily policed part of the city. That cuts both ways, and both halves matter. The enforcement is real: in the first half of 2026 police recorded close to 40,000 identity checks and around 120 removal orders in the station and Bolognina area, and reported crime there fell 58.3% year on year, with robberies down 75%, thefts down 74.4% and drug offences down 31.2%. But a decline that steep measures how high the baseline was, and the area is still the one the city assigns extra officers and cameras to. Treat it as an ordinary big-city station district: fine to stay in, worth the usual care at night.

zones.name: San Donato-San Vitale
zones.text: The quartiere that holds both of Bologna's most-reported problem areas, which is why it is rated hardest. Piazza Verdi and via Zamboni — the heart of the university quarter, and a street most visitors walk to reach the Due Torri — are covered continuously by Il Resto del Carlino and BolognaToday for street dealing, night-time disorder and assaults; traders on via Zamboni have publicly described the situation as out of control, and the city runs repeated anti-degrado operations in the square. Further out, the Pilastro estate is a standing item at the Prefettura's provincial security committee, which reports constant territorial policing there. San Donato itself is described in local coverage as one of the city's most difficult areas, with dealing and juvenile crime. In daylight the university streets are simply busy and full of students; the rating is for after dark.

zones.name: Santo Stefano
zones.text: The south-eastern centre and the hills above it: Piazza Santo Stefano, Strada Maggiore, via Castiglione and the Giardini Margherita, and the most expensive address in Bologna. What local sources do document here is property crime rather than anything directed at people — smash-and-grab raids on shops along via Santo Stefano, and burglaries of houses on the hills, which is what the Comune's neighbourhood-watch pact with the Comicolli association (valid to 31 December 2026) was set up to address. Neither is a reason for a visitor to avoid the area at any hour.

zones.name: Porto-Saragozza
zones.text: The western half of the centre plus Saragozza and the start of the portico up to San Luca: well-off, and the part of the centre most visitors find pleasant. The one documented qualifier is nightlife rather than crime — via del Pratello is the city's densest bar street and generates the noise and drunkenness complaints that come with that. The quartiere's hillside edge is inside the neighbourhood-watch pact the Comune signed with the Comicolli residents' association, which runs to 31 December 2026 and exists because of burglaries of houses on the hills — a resident's problem, not a visitor's.

zones.name: Savena
zones.text: Residential south-east, outside the walls: post-war housing, the Parco dei Cedri, and very little that draws visitors. The only finding in local and municipal sources is that its foothill edge is covered by the same Comune neighbourhood-watch pact against house burglary as the hills of Santo Stefano and Porto-Saragozza. Quiet rather than empty, and quiet at night too.
